title: Propositions and Connectives
quickIdea: A proposition is a declarative statement that is either true or false, never both. Connectives join propositions into compound propositions whose truth value depends only on the parts.
remember: Proposition = declarative statement with exactly one truth value. 'Statement' is a synonym.
Not propositions: questions, commands, exclamations, paradoxes, and sentences with a free variable such as 'x > 5'.
Context must be fixed first: 'this rose is white' is a proposition once the rose is fixed.
Basic connectives: not, and, or, implies, iff. Exclusive or is derived: p xor q = (p or q) and not (p and q).
Precedence, tightest first: not, and, or, implies, iff. Bracket when unsure - precedence is a trap, not a shortcut.
AND is true only when both parts are true; OR is true unless both parts are false; XOR is true when exactly one part is true.

example.prompt: Which of these are propositions? (a) 6 < 24  (b) triangles have four vertices  (c) close the door  (d) x + 1 = 3
example.work: (a) is declarative and true, so it is a proposition. (b) is declarative and false - still a proposition, because false is a truth value. (c) is a command with no truth value, so it is not a proposition. (d) contains a free variable, so it becomes a proposition only after x is fixed.

gateAngle: GATE tests translation, not definitions. Two patterns recur: turn an English sentence into symbols (2024 Set 2 Q.12: 'fail grade cannot be given when the student scores more than 50%' is q -> not p), and pick the one formula that is not equivalent to the rest.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: Let p: the file is corrupted, q: the backup exists. Write 'the file is not corrupted unless the backup does not exist' in symbols.
variations.why: 'A unless B' means 'if not B then A'. Here A = not p and B = not q, so not (not q) -> not p, that is q -> not p. Reading 'unless' as plain AND is the standard error.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Which of these are not propositions: (i) 7 is prime  (ii) x is prime  (iii) 7 is prime, isn't it?  (iv) 2 + 2 = 5
variations.why: (ii) has a free variable, so it has no truth value until x is fixed. (iii) is a question, not a declaration. (i) is true and (iv) is false, so both are propositions - being false does not stop something being a proposition.

trap.what: Reading 'only if', 'if', 'when' and 'unless' backwards, and assuming the converse is the same statement.
trap.why: 'p only if q' is p -> q, but 'p if q' is q -> p. The two directions are different statements, and only the contrapositive is equivalent to the original.
trap.counterexample: GATE 1998 Q.1.5 asks for the converse of 'I stay only if you go'. The assertion is P -> Q with P = 'I stay', Q = 'you go'; its converse is Q -> P, 'I stay if you go', not the original.

check.question: Are 'if it rains, the match is not played' and 'it rains only if the match is not played' the same formula?
check.answer: Yes, both are R -> not P.
check.explanation: 'if R then S' is R -> S, and 'R only if S' is also R -> S. What differs is 'R if S', which is S -> R.
